entry.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part III)

link.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part III)

entry.content:
Part 11 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Classifying and Finding New Possible Orbits

This post continues the problem of two fixed centres from part 4 and part 6.

New types of orbits

The run in part 6 started from rest and stayed around one of the two centres, so \(S = \cos\sigma\) covered only part of its range. Giving the body an initial velocity produces two further types of orbit, lemniscate and planetary.

To classify them, we need two constants of motion. With the centres at \((\pm d, 0)\) and masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\),

\[\begin{aligned} G&=\frac{1}{2}\left(x p_y-y p_x\right)^2+\frac{1}{2} d^2 p_x^2 \\ &\quad+d x\Biggl(\frac{m_1}{\sqrt{(x+d)^2+y^2}} \\ &\qquad-\frac{m_2}{\sqrt{(x-d)^2+y^2}}\Biggr), \\ H&=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_x^2+p_y^2\right) \\ &\quad-\frac{m_1}{\sqrt{(x+d)^2+y^2}}-\frac{m_2}{\sqrt{(x-d)^2+y^2}} . \end{aligned}\]

\(H\) is the energy, and \(G\) is the additional constant of motion discovered by Euler, which makes the problem integrable. The mass of the moving body drops out of the equations of motion, so \(p_x\) and \(p_y\) are momenta per unit mass.

The paper Syzygies in the Two Center Problem shows that the values of \(H\) and \(G\) determine the type of orbit: \(S\) (satellite, the type found in part 6), \(L\) (lemniscate) and \(P\) (planetary).

My simulations reproduce all three types:

Why a body released from rest stays on one side

For equal masses, the equation for \(S\) from part 4 can be written with these two constants. Let \(R\) be the mean of the distances to the two centres, so that \(S = x/R\), and let \(f\) be the variable defined by \(df = dt/(R^2 - d^2 S^2)\). Then

\[\left(\frac{dS}{df}\right)^2 = 2G\left(1-S^2\right)\left(1-\frac{H d^2}{G}\, S^2\right).\]

A body released from rest has no kinetic terms in \(G\), which leaves \(G = d\,x\,(m_1/r_1 - m_2/r_2)\). This is negative on either side of the line \(x = 0\), because the nearer centre has the larger \(m/r\). With \(G\) and \(H\) both negative, the right-hand side is non-negative only where

\[S^2 \ge \frac{G}{H d^2},\]

so \(S\) never reaches zero and the body never crosses to the other side, whatever its energy. That is the satellite orbit of part 6, and it is why starting from rest could not give anything else. As a check, a body released from rest at \((1.6, 1.2)\), with \(d = 1\) and unit masses, has \(G = -0.634\) and \(H = -1.095\). The bound is \(\lvert S\rvert \ge 0.761\), and in the simulation \(S\) stays between 0.761 and 1.

When \(G > 0\) the right-hand side is positive for every \(\lvert S\rvert < 1\), so \(S\) sweeps the whole interval. These are the lemniscate and planetary orbits. They differ in whether \(R\) comes down to \(d\), that is, whether the body passes between the centres.

S follows sn in the right variable

With the new orbits \(S\) covers its full range, but against time it looks irregular:

In 2024 I could not see \(\operatorname{sn}\) in this plot. The reason is that the solution is a function of \(f\) and not of \(t\). The two are related by \(dt = (R^2 - d^2 S^2)\, df\), so a given step in \(f\) takes little time when the body is close to the centres and a long time when it is far away. Against \(f\) the oscillation is exactly periodic, and it is the Jacobi function

\[S = \operatorname{sn}\left(\sqrt{2G}\, f + \omega \,\middle|\, k\right), \qquad k^2 = \frac{H d^2}{G} .\]

For this orbit \(k^2 = -0.324\). A bound orbit with \(G > 0\) always has \(k^2 < 0\), an imaginary modulus, for which \(\operatorname{sn}\) is still real and periodic.

Next steps

  • Map out which initial conditions lead to each of \(S\), \(L\) and \(P\).
  • Extend the analysis to unequal fixed masses, where the equation for \(S\) gains a term linear in \(S\).

The comparison of simulated orbits with \(G\) and \(H\) was later written up as a short paper, An Analysis of the Restricted Euler Problem Using Symplectic Integrators.

Credits

This post draws on Syzygies in the Two Center Problem and the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna.

Revised on 25 October and 11 November 2026. The original quoted values of the book’s parameter \(e\) for the three orbits (2.5, 0.98 and 1.08). They came from a bug in the code that computed them and are removed. The original also left two things open: why \(S\) did not look like \(\operatorname{sn}\), and whether the mass of the moving body matters. Both are now answered in the text. The equation for \(S\) in terms of \(G\) and \(H\), the argument about bodies released from rest and the last figure were added in the second revision.
entry.summary: Two constants of motion sort the orbits of the two-centre problem into satellite, lemniscate and planetary types, and explain why a body released from rest stays on one side.

entry.title: Classifying and Finding New Possible Orbits

link.title: Classifying and Finding New Possible Orbits

entry.content:
Part 10 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere
Next: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part III)

This post describes a first systematic search for interesting orbits: a scan over a family of initial conditions, recording which ones keep the three bodies together.

Set-up

Take three unit masses, \(m_1 = m_2 = m_3 = 1\), and \(G=1\). Start them on a line with zero total momentum and zero angular momentum:

Body Initial position Initial velocity
1 \((-1, 0)\) \((a, b)\)
2 \((1, 0)\) \((a, b)\)
3 \((0, 0)\) \((-2a, -2b)\)

This is the standard family that contains the figure-eight orbit, at about \((a,b) = (0.347, 0.533)\).

I varied \(a\) and \(b\) independently from \(0\) to \(1\) in steps of \(0.01\), which gives \(10\,201\) runs. Each run takes \(50\,000\) steps of \(\Delta t = 0.001\), or 50 time units. A run fails as soon as the bodies are too far apart. Otherwise it passes, and the point \((a, b)\) is plotted.

Results

Around the figure-eight orbit, the outcome is more sensitive to changes in the vertical velocity \(b\) than to changes in \(a\). This agrees with the findings of an earlier Edinburgh vacation-project report by F. Ramos.

A finer scan of that region (about 15 hours), with the figure-eight marked in red:

What the scan measured

In November 2026 I ran the scan again, this time recording the energy of every run. The first figure is reproduced, with 97% of the plotted area in common, when a run is stopped once two bodies are more than 100 apart. In 2024 I quoted the limit as 20 from the origin; with that limit the outer band would be missing, so the figure was made with the larger one.

The total energy of this family is

\[E = 3\left(a^2+b^2\right) - \tfrac{5}{2},\]

because the kinetic energy is \(3(a^2+b^2)\) and the three pairs start at distances 2, 1 and 1. It is positive outside the circle \(a^2+b^2 = \tfrac56\), of radius 0.913. With positive energy the bodies cannot stay together: the moment of inertia \(I = \sum_i \lvert\mathbf r_i\rvert^2\) obeys the Lagrange–Jacobi identity \(\ddot I = 4E - 2V\), and \(V < 0\), so \(I\) grows without limit. Yet the dense band in the figure reaches \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2} = 1.1\). Those runs pass only because 50 time units is too short for the bodies to move 100 apart. Of the \(4\,539\) points that pass, 43% have positive energy.

Inside the circle, \(4\,056\) runs fail, and in all but three of them the energy changed by more than its own magnitude. A close encounter that a step of \(0.001\) cannot resolve gave one body a kick, and that body then left. Whether those systems would really have broken up, the run cannot say. The passes thin out towards small \(a\) and \(b\) because bodies that start slowly fall almost straight towards each other.

So outside the circle the scan measured how quickly unbound systems separate, and inside it whether a fixed step survived the close encounters. The band around the figure-eight is the part that holds up. At the nearest grid point, \((0.35, 0.53)\), no two bodies are ever more than 2.01 apart and the energy varies by \(2.5 \times 10^{-12}\) of its value.

Why a distance limit is not enough

Even with exact integration, a distance limit cannot separate bound motion from escape. In the two-body problem, negative energy forces a bounded orbit. With three bodies, two of them can form a tight binary whose potential energy is arbitrarily negative, which leaves the third body enough energy to travel arbitrarily far, and possibly return, while the total energy stays negative. With unit masses and \(G = 1\), the potential energy is

\[V = -\left(\frac{1}{r_{12}} + \frac{1}{r_{23}} + \frac{1}{r_{13}}\right),\]

and making one separation small makes \(V\) as negative as we like, whatever the other two separations are.

The return proximity function

A more targeted test, introduced by Šuvakov and Dmitrašinović, looks for orbits that come back close to where they started in phase space. The return proximity function \(P(t)\) is the distance between the state at time \(t\) and the initial state,

\[P(t)^2=\sum_{i=1}^3\left\lvert\mathbf{r}_i(t)-\mathbf{r}_i(0)\right\rvert^2+\sum_{i=1}^3\left\lvert\mathbf{p}_i(t) - \mathbf{p}_i(0)\right\rvert^2 .\]

For a periodic orbit \(P\) returns to zero after each period, so a small minimum of \(P\) over \(t > 0\) marks a candidate. My plan at this point was to keep the orbits with \(P<15\) throughout the run and \(\min_{t > 0} P(t) < 0.7\). The search the project ended with used a separation limit of 5 and a test on the energy instead. The write-up analyses that search and maps the closest return over the whole family.

Cost

The scan is \(10\,201\) runs of \(50\,000\) steps, \(5 \times 10^8\) steps in all, and took 32 hours: about \(4\,400\) steps per second. The rerun advances all the runs together as NumPy arrays and takes two minutes on a laptop.

Credits

This search is inspired by the paper New Families of Periodic Orbits for the Planar Three-Body Problem Computed with High Precision. The return proximity function is from M. Šuvakov and V. Dmitrašinović, Three classes of Newtonian three-body planar periodic orbits, Phys. Rev. Lett. 110, 114301 (2013).

Revised on 25 October and 11 November 2026. The original had these errors:

  • The initial conditions put the body with velocity \(-2(a, b)\) at \((1, 0)\). The figure-eight values quoted, \((a, b) \approx (0.35, 0.53)\), belong to the standard arrangement with that body at the origin, which the table now gives.
  • The potential energy was written \(1/a + 1/b + 1/c\). Gravitational potential energy is negative: \(V = -(1/r_{12} + 1/r_{23} + 1/r_{13})\).
  • The argument for why no cut-off radius works did not hold up. The real reason is that two bodies can form a tight binary with arbitrarily negative potential energy, which leaves the third body enough energy to travel arbitrarily far.
  • The return proximity function compared the momenta with zero instead of with their initial values.
  • The limit on the distance was given as 20 from the origin. The figure corresponds to a limit of 100 between two bodies.

The section on what the scan measured and the note on its cost come from the rerun and were added in the second revision. The first revision still called the points that passed bounded. The title originally ended in “(Part I)”.
entry.summary: A scan over the initial velocities of three equal masses. A rerun shows that 43% of the runs that passed were unbound, and that the failures came from the fixed time step.

entry.title: Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere

link.title: Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere

entry.content:
Part 9 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II)
Next: Classifying and Finding New Possible Orbits

This post outlines the proof that the figure-eight orbit exists, following Chenciner and Montgomery. It uses the shape sphere together with the direct method of the calculus of variations.

Outline of the proof

  1. Minimise the action over paths that start at an Euler configuration (three bodies collinear, one at the midpoint of the other two) and end at an isosceles configuration. The minimiser is one twelfth of the orbit.
  2. Show that the minimiser has no collisions. Let \(A_2\) be a lower bound for the action of any path with a collision, and exhibit a collision-free test path whose action is smaller than \(A_2\). Then the minimiser cannot collide.
  3. Use the symmetries of the equal-mass problem to make twelve copies of this arc, and show that they join smoothly into one closed curve in the space of triangles up to rotation.
  4. Reconstruct the motion in the plane from that curve, and show that the three bodies follow a single figure-eight-shaped curve.

The figure eight is special: numerical work by Simó indicates that it is stable, which is very rare among choreographies (orbits in which all the bodies follow the same curve). By contrast, Lagrange’s equilateral circular orbit with three equal masses is a choreography too, but it is unstable (see Routh’s criterion in part 8).

Step 1: finding minimisers

Following Chenciner and Montgomery, define the action

\[A = \int_{0}^{T} \left(\tfrac{1}{2}K+U\right) dt ,\]

where \(K = \lvert\dot x\rvert^2\) is twice the kinetic energy and \(U\) is the force function (the negative of the potential energy). The action is minimised over the set \(\Lambda\) of paths in the Sobolev space \(H^1([0,T], X)\) that start at an Euler configuration (of arbitrary size) and end at an isosceles configuration. Here

\[X = \left\{ x=(x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \mathbb{C}^3 \;\middle|\; \sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i =0 \right\},\]

and \(H^1\) consists of paths that, together with their time derivatives, are square integrable, which is the right setting for the direct method. Throughout, \(T\) is the duration of this arc, one twelfth of the period of the final orbit.

The conditions at the two ends do not change when the triangle is rotated, so a minimiser can be taken to have zero angular momentum: any rotation of the triangle along the way adds kinetic energy without changing \(U\). The problem then lives in the space of triangles up to rotation, which is \(\mathbb{R}^3\), a cone over the shape sphere with the size of the triangle as the radial direction.

That a minimiser exists is standard. The difficulty is that for Newton’s \(1/r\) potential a path that runs into a collision still has finite action, so nothing so far prevents the minimiser from being such a path.

Step 2: the minimiser has no collisions

Collisions are expensive

If a path in \(\Lambda\) has a collision (double or triple), its action is at least \(A_2\), where \(A_2\) is the action of the collinear two-body solution in which two unit masses start at collision and come to rest a time \(T\) later, with the centre of mass fixed. The reason is that removing the third mass can only lower the action, and for two bodies a theorem of Gordon identifies the cheapest path with a collision. Explicitly,

\[A_2 = \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{\pi^2\, T}{2}\right)^{1/3} .\]

A cheaper test path

The test path keeps the moment of inertia fixed at a value \(I_0\) and moves at constant speed along the level curve of \(U\) through the Euler configuration, from the Euler configuration to the isosceles one. Its length is \(\ell_0 \sqrt{I_0}\), where \(\ell_0\), the Euler equipotential length, is the length of the same curve on the shape sphere \(I = 1\). Both terms of the action are constant along this path, and choosing \(I_0\) to minimise their sum gives

\[a = \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{25\, \ell_0^2\, T}{2}\right)^{1/3} .\]

Comparing the two formulas, \(a < A_2\) exactly when \(\ell_0 < \pi/5\). The length has to be computed numerically: Simó found \(\ell_0 = \pi/5.0826\), later confirmed by Laskar, so the inequality holds with a margin of 1.6%.

Conclusion

Putting these together,

\[\min_{\Lambda} A \;\le\; a \;<\; A_2 \;\le\; A(\text{any colliding path}),\]

so the minimiser is collision-free. With the period normalised to \(2\pi\), so that \(T = \pi/6\), the paper quotes \(A_2 = 2.0583\) and \(a = 2.0360\), and Simó’s numerical value for the minimum itself is \(2.0310\). The test path is within 0.25% of the true minimum and about 1% below the collision bound.

Step 3: assembling the full orbit

The main difficulty is to show that the copies fit together smoothly at their endpoints.

In the space of triangles up to rotation, the Euler configurations with body 3 in the middle form a ray \(E_3\) from the origin, and the isosceles configurations with \(r_{12} = r_{13}\) form a half-plane \(M_1\). On the shape sphere they appear as a point and a meridian. The arc starts somewhere on \(E_3\) and ends somewhere on \(M_1\), and the first task is to show that it meets both at right angles. Recall the first variation of the action:

\[\delta A = \epsilon \left[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\, \eta \right]_0^T + \epsilon \int_0^T \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} - \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\right) \eta \, dt .\]

Usually the boundary term vanishes because the endpoints are fixed, so \(\eta(0)=\eta(T)=0\). Here the endpoints may slide along \(E_3\) and within \(M_1\), so \(\eta\) need not vanish there. The integral vanishes because the minimiser satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations, so we need

\[\left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\right|_{t=0} \cdot \eta(0) = 0, \qquad \left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}}\right|_{t=T} \cdot \eta(T) = 0\]

for every allowed \(\eta\). For this Lagrangian \(\partial L/\partial \dot{x}\) is the velocity \(\dot{x}\), and \(\eta\) can be any vector tangent to \(E_3\) at \(t = 0\) or to \(M_1\) at \(t = T\), so the arc leaves \(E_3\) and arrives at \(M_1\) at right angles.

Reflection in \(M_1\) corresponds to exchanging bodies 2 and 3 and mirroring the plane, which is a symmetry when the masses are equal. The mirror image of the arc, run backwards in time, is therefore also a solution. Because the arc reaches \(M_1\) at a right angle, the mirrored arc sets off from the same point with the same velocity, and by uniqueness of solutions it is the continuation of the original arc. The same argument applies at the Euler end with a half-turn about the ray. Repeating it gives twelve arcs that form one smooth closed solution curve.

Step 4: from the shape sphere back to the plane

Periodicity

Suppose the curve on the shape sphere is closed. Then the initial and final triangles in the plane are similar, because they correspond to the same point of the shape sphere, and it remains to find the angle of rotation between them.

For motions with zero angular momentum, the area rule gives it: the rotation angle equals twice the spherical area enclosed by the shape curve (on the shape sphere of radius \(\tfrac12\), as normalised by Chenciner and Montgomery).

The figure below defines the points \(E_i\) on the equator (the collinear configurations with body \(i\) in the middle) and the meridian \(M_1\):

Combining the area rule with the symmetries shows that the motion in the plane is periodic and that the three bodies move along the same curve, one third of a period apart:

No extra loops

Finally, one shows that the angular momentum of each individual body about the centre of mass vanishes only when that body passes through the origin. So each body’s polar angle changes monotonically on each lobe, and each lobe is star-shaped: the curve has no extra loops. The curve traced out is therefore a figure eight.

Credits

This proof is not original. It follows A. Chenciner and R. Montgomery, A remarkable periodic solution of the three-body problem in the case of equal masses, Annals of Mathematics 152 (2000), 881–901, and the presentation I’ve Got a Three-Body Problem by Gareth E. Roberts (College of the Holy Cross, 2008).

Revised on 25 October and 11 November 2026. The outline stated the key step the wrong way round. It said to show that every collision-free path has a smaller action than the cheapest path with a collision. What the proof needs is one collision-free test path whose action is below a lower bound for all paths with collisions; then the minimiser cannot collide. The outline is rewritten in numbered steps, and the configuration space is written \(X\) instead of \(\chi\). The second revision added the formulas and numerical values of the actions from the paper, the reason the minimiser has zero angular momentum, and the reflection argument that joins the arcs. Previously titled “A Proof of the Existence of the Figure-8 Orbit using Actions and the Shape Sphere”.
entry.summary: An outline of Chenciner and Montgomery's variational proof: minimise the action over one twelfth of the orbit, rule out collisions, and assemble the figure eight.

entry.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II)

link.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II)

entry.content:
Part 8 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I)
Next: Proving the Figure-Eight Orbit Exists: Action Minimisation on the Shape Sphere

Continuing from part 7, this post estimates how many terms of Sundman’s series are needed in a simple example, and shows why the series is useless in practice.

Lagrange’s equilateral solution

In 1772 Lagrange found a family of solutions in which the three bodies form an equilateral triangle at every instant. In the restricted problem, the small body then sits at one of the \(L_4\) or \(L_5\) Lagrange points, also called Trojan points.

The configuration is linearly stable only when one mass dominates. In the restricted problem, the two large masses must differ by a factor of more than about \(25\) (Routh’s criterion: a mass ratio above \(24.96\)). Otherwise any small perturbation grows and the triangle breaks up:

Estimating the number of terms

In the unperturbed solution each body moves on a circle, which we parametrise as \((x,y) = (\cos t, \sin t)\).

The mutual distances stay constant, say equal to \(r\), so Sundman’s factor

\[\Gamma = \left(1-e^{-r/l}\right)^3\]

is constant too, and \(t=\Gamma w\). Using the map from the previous post,

\[\begin{aligned} t&=\frac{2 \Omega \Gamma}{\pi} \log \frac{1+\tau}{1-\tau} \\ &= 2A\left(\tau + \frac{\tau^3}{3} + \frac{\tau^5}{5}+ O(\tau^7)\right), \\ \text{with}\quad A &= \frac{2\Omega\Gamma}{\pi} . \end{aligned}\]

Substituting into the Taylor series of \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) gives the coordinates as power series in \(\tau\):

\[\begin{aligned} \cos t &= 1 - 2A^2 \tau^2 - \left(\tfrac{4}{3} A^2 - \tfrac{2}{3} A^4\right) \tau^4 \\ &\quad - \left(\tfrac{46}{45}A^2 - \tfrac{8}{9} A^4 + \tfrac{4}{45} A^6\right) \tau^6+O(\tau^8), \\ \sin t &= 2A \tau + \left(\tfrac{2}{3}A - \tfrac{4}{3} A^3\right) \tau^3 \\ &\quad + \left(\tfrac{2}{5}A - \tfrac{4}{3}A^3 + \tfrac{4}{15} A^5\right) \tau^5 + O(\tau^7) . \end{aligned}\]

Now take masses \((m_0, m_1, m_2) = \left(\tfrac{1}{200}, \tfrac{1}{200}, \tfrac{99}{100}\right)\). For this configuration \(\Omega < 9 \times 10^{-8}\), which gives \(A < 4 \times 10^{-8}\).

How many terms do we need to follow the motion up to \(t = 1\)? Truncating the series for \(t\) after \(n\) terms, to get within \(0.1\) of \(t = 1\) we need

\[\begin{gathered} 2A \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\tau^{2k-1}}{2k-1} > 0.9, \\ \text{i.e.}\quad S_\tau := \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\tau^{2k-1}}{2k-1} > \frac{9}{20A} . \end{gathered}\]

With \(A< 4 \times 10^{-8}\) this requires \(S_\tau > 10^7\).

Compare with the partial sums of the odd harmonic series,

\[S_p=\sum_{k=1}^{p} \frac{1}{2k-1} \approx \tfrac12 \ln p + \text{const}.\]

Reaching \(S_p > S\) requires \(p>e^{2S-2.4}\), so \(S_p > 10^7\) requires \(p > 10^{8 \times 10^{6}}\). Since \(\lvert\tau\rvert < 1\), each term of \(S_\tau\) is smaller than the corresponding term of \(S_p\), so \(S_\tau\) needs at least as many terms: \(n > p > 10^{8 \times 10^{6}}\).

So even in this simple, collision-free example, about \(10^{8\,000\,000}\) terms are needed for one decimal place of accuracy. Sundman’s series converges, but far too slowly ever to be used.

Credits

This post is based on D. K. Yeomans’s exposition of Sundman’s work and on Belorizky’s paper (1930).

Revised on 25 October 2026. The original had these errors:

  • In the series for \(\cos t\), the coefficient \(\tfrac{46}{45}\) was written \(\tfrac{45}{46}\).
  • The factor \(\Gamma\) was written with \(e^{1/l}\) instead of \(e^{-r/l}\).
  • The sum \(\sum_{k=1}^{p} \frac{1}{2k-1}\) had \(2p-1\) in the denominator, and the error term after \(\tau^5\) is \(O(\tau^7)\), not \(O(\tau^6)\).
  • A reference link no longer worked.

All are fixed, and the estimate of the number of terms is explained step by step.
entry.summary: Applying Sundman's series to Lagrange's equilateral solution shows why it is impractical: it needs more than 10 to the power 8 million terms for one digit of accuracy.

entry.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I)

link.title: Sundman’s Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I)

entry.content:
Part 7 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II)
Next: Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part II)

In 1912 Karl F. Sundman found a convergent power-series solution to the three-body problem, valid whenever the total angular momentum is non-zero. In principle this is a general solution, but its convergence is so slow that it is of no practical use. This post outlines how it works.

Key points of Sundman’s paper

  • At a double (binary) collision, the distance to the third, non-colliding body stays bounded.
  • A triple collision can only occur if the total angular momentum (the “area integral”) is zero.
  • At a double collision, the velocities and accelerations of the colliding bodies tend to infinity.
  • The unit vector along the line joining the two colliding bodies tends to a limit.
  • The singularity of a collision between a given pair of bodies can be removed by introducing a new independent variable \(u\).
  • A different independent variable \(w\) removes all the double-collision singularities at once, allowing any number and combination of double collisions.
  • The coordinates of the three bodies can then be expanded as power series in \(w\).
  • These series converge for all time, although extremely slowly.

The regularising variable \(w\)

Where the singularities come from

The variable \(u\) regularises a collision between one particular pair of bodies, say \(m_0\) and \(m_1\). The equations of motion contain terms such as \(1/r_0\) and \(1/r_1\), where the \(r_i\) are mutual distances, so a collision involving a different pair still produces a singularity. We need a variable that treats all three pairs symmetrically.

Definition

Sundman’s variable \(w\) is defined by

\[dt= \Gamma\, dw, \qquad w=0 \text{ at } t=0,\]

where

\[\Gamma = \left(1-e^{-r_0/l}\right)\left(1-e^{-r_1/l}\right)\left(1-e^{-r_2/l}\right)\]

for a suitable constant \(l\), and \(r_0, r_1, r_2\) are the three mutual distances. The definition is symmetric in the three distances, so every double collision is regularised in the same way.

Convergence in a strip

After a long analysis (Yeomans gives a complete account), one finds that the coordinates are holomorphic functions of \(w\) in a strip around the real axis,

\[\lvert \operatorname{Im} w\rvert < \Omega,\]

for some \(\Omega > 0\): a strip of width \(2\Omega\).

Mapping the strip to a disc

A power series converges in a disc, not a strip, so we map the strip conformally onto the unit disc.

Write the strip as \(S = \{s : \lvert\operatorname{Im} s\rvert < \beta\}\). The exponential map

\[g(s) = e^{\pi s / (2\beta)}\]

sends \(S\) onto the right half-plane \(\{\operatorname{Re} z > 0\}\). Points of the right half-plane are closer to \(1\) than to \(-1\), i.e. \(\lvert z-1\rvert < \lvert z+1\rvert\), so the Möbius transformation

\[h(z)=\frac{z-1}{z+1}\]

maps the right half-plane onto the unit disc. The composition \(h \circ g\) therefore maps \(S\) onto the unit disc. With \(\beta = \Omega\), the new variable \(\tau = h(g(w))\) satisfies

\[w = \frac{2 \Omega}{\pi} \log\frac{1+ \tau}{1- \tau},\]

and the coordinates become power series in \(\tau\) that converge for \(\lvert\tau\rvert < 1\). The whole real time axis, \(-\infty < w < \infty\), corresponds to the real interval \(-1 < \tau < 1\).

This is also the source of the slow convergence: late times are squeezed towards the boundary \(\lvert\tau\rvert = 1\) of the disc of convergence, where power series converge very slowly.

When does it work?

The series exist whenever the total angular momentum is non-zero,

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{c} &= m_0 (\mathbf{r}_0 \times \mathbf{v}_0) + m_1 (\mathbf{r}_1\times \mathbf{v}_1) \\ &\quad+ m_2 ( \mathbf{r}_2 \times \mathbf{v}_2) \neq \mathbf{0} . \end{aligned}\]

That covers essentially every case, including double collisions, but not triple collisions, which require \(\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}\).

The difficulty is the rate of convergence. Belorizky estimated that something like \(10^{8\,000\,000}\) terms would be needed for useful accuracy in a simple case. Part 8 goes through the estimate.

Summary

Sundman found an independent variable \(w\) in which every double collision is regular. The solution is analytic in a strip of width \(2\Omega\) around the real \(w\)-axis, which a conformal map sends to the unit disc in a new variable \(\tau\). The resulting power series in \(\tau\) solve the three-body problem for all time whenever the angular momentum is non-zero, but they converge far too slowly to be useful.

A Broucke–Hadjidemetriou–Hénon orbit

Alongside the reading, I simulated orbits of the Broucke–Hadjidemetriou–Hénon (BHH) family. Here is one, with its curve on the shape sphere seen from two angles:

Credits

This post is based on D. K. Yeomans’s exposition of Sundman’s regularisation of the three-body problem, NASA technical memorandum X-640-66-481 (1966), and on notes by Peter Senchyna.

Revised on 25 October 2026. The original had these errors:

  • The map from the right half-plane to the unit disc was written \(h(z) = \lvert z-1\rvert / \lvert z+1\rvert\), which is a number, not a map. It is the Möbius transformation \(h(z) = (z-1)/(z+1)\).
  • The strip was written \(\operatorname{Im} s \le \beta\) instead of \(\lvert\operatorname{Im} s\rvert < \beta\).
  • A reference link no longer worked.

All are fixed, and the reference now points to the copy on NASA’s Technical Reports Server.
entry.summary: Sundman's 1912 series solves the three-body problem for non-zero angular momentum. How the regularising variable works, and why the series is useless in practice.

entry.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II)

link.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II)

entry.content:
Part 6 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere
Next: Sundman's Power Series Solution to the Three-Body Problem (Part I)

This post continues the problem of two fixed centres, introduced in part 4, by converting my simulated trajectories into the coordinates in which the theory is written.

From Cartesian to prolate spheroidal coordinates

Recall the prolate spheroidal coordinates \((R, \sigma)\), with the centres at distance \(b\) from the origin and \(\sigma \in [0, \pi]\):

\[x= \pm \sqrt{R^2-b^2}\, \sin \sigma, \qquad z=R \cos \sigma .\]

The sign of \(x\) is carried by the \(\pm\), so it is enough to consider \(x \geq 0\). Take \(b = 1\).

Substituting \(R = z/\cos\sigma\) into the first equation and squaring,

\[\begin{aligned} x^2 &= \sin^2 \sigma \left(\frac{z^2}{\cos^2 \sigma} - 1\right) = \frac{(z^2 - \cos^2 \sigma)\sin^2 \sigma}{\cos^2 \sigma} \\ &= \frac{(z^2 - 1 + \sin^2 \sigma)\sin^2 \sigma}{1 - \sin^2 \sigma}, \end{aligned}\]

which rearranges to

\[x^2 = \sin^2 \sigma \left(x^2 + z^2 - 1 + \sin^2 \sigma\right).\]

(This step divides by \(\cos\sigma\), so it fails on the line \(z = 0\), which has to be handled separately.) Setting \(u=\sin^2\sigma\) gives a quadratic,

\[u^2+(x^2+z^2-1)\,u-x^2=0,\]

whose non-negative root is

\[u = \frac{-(x^2 + z^2 - 1) + \sqrt{(x^2 + z^2 - 1)^2 + 4x^2}}{2} .\]

Then \(\sigma_1 = \arcsin\sqrt{u}\) lies in \([0, \pi/2]\). Since \(z = R\cos\sigma\) with \(R \ge 0\), this is the correct angle when \(z \ge 0\); when \(z<0\) the angle lies in \((\pi/2, \pi]\), and we take \(\sigma = \pi - \sigma_1\):

\[\sigma = \begin{cases} \sigma_1, & z \ge 0, \\ \pi - \sigma_1, & z < 0. \end{cases}\]

Given \(\sigma\), \(R = z/\cos\sigma\) follows immediately (or \(R = \sqrt{x^2/\sin^2\sigma + b^2}\) near \(z = 0\)).

Results

For this trajectory:

the coordinate \(R\) evolves as

the angle \(\sigma\) as

and \(S = \cos\sigma\) as

Interpretation

The moving body never passes between the two centres. It stays around one of them, so \(S = \cos\sigma\) covers only part of the interval \([-1, 1]\), whereas the \(\operatorname{sn}\) solution quoted in part 4 sweeps the whole interval.

At the time I read this as a disagreement with the theory. It is not one. This run started from rest, and with two equal centres a body released from rest always stays on its own side: it is a satellite orbit, bound to a single centre. Part 11 derives this from the second constant of motion and finds the orbits that pass around both centres, which need an initial velocity.

Credits

This post is based on the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna.

Revised on 25 October and 11 November 2026. The discussion of which branch of \(\arcsin\) to take described \(\sigma\) in the range \(\pi/2 < \sigma < 3\pi/2\), but in these coordinates \(\sigma\) only runs from 0 to \(\pi\). The rule is now stated directly: \(\sigma = \sigma_1\) when \(z \ge 0\) and \(\sigma = \pi - \sigma_1\) when \(z < 0\). The last section originally took the limited range of \(S\) as a disagreement with the theory and suggested giving the fixed centres very large masses instead of holding them in place. Holding them fixed is correct, and the limited range is what a satellite orbit shows.
entry.summary: Converting simulated trajectories from Cartesian to prolate spheroidal coordinates, and why the first results disagreed with the theory.

entry.title: Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere

link.title: Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere

entry.content:
Part 5 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I)
Next: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part II)

This post introduces the shape sphere, a way to picture the motion of three bodies by keeping track only of the shape of the triangle they form.

Reducing the three-body problem

Reduction simplifies the three-body problem by removing degrees of freedom associated with symmetries.

Let the three bodies lie in the plane, identified with \(\mathbb{C}\). Before reduction, the configuration space is \(\mathbb{C}^3\), the positions of the three masses. By Galilean invariance we can fix the centre of mass at the origin, which reduces the configuration space to

\[X = \left\{ x = (x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \mathbb{C}^3 \;\middle|\; \sum_{i=1}^3 x_i = 0 \right\} \cong \mathbb{C}^2 .\]

Next come the rotations and reflections of the plane, which act by

\[\begin{aligned} R_\theta \cdot (x_1, x_2, x_3) &= (e^{i\theta} x_1, e^{i\theta} x_2, e^{i\theta} x_3), \\ S \cdot (x_1, x_2, x_3) &= (\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2, \bar{x}_3). \end{aligned}\]

Taking the quotient of \(X\) by the rotation group \(SO(2)\) gives a space homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^3\), whose points are oriented congruence classes of triangles. Fixing the overall size as well, by setting the moment of inertia to \(I = 1\), leaves a 2-sphere whose points are oriented similarity classes of triangles: the shape sphere.

The maps

For equal masses, the Jacobi map \(\mathcal{J}: X \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^2\) is

\[\begin{aligned} \left(z_1, z_2\right)&=\mathcal{J}\left(x_1, x_2, x_3\right) \\ &=\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x_3-x_2),\ \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\bigl(x_1-\tfrac{1}{2}(x_2+x_3)\bigr)\Bigr), \end{aligned}\]

and the Hopf map \(\mathcal{K}: \mathbb{C}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}^3\) is

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal{K}\left(z_1, z_2\right)&=\left(u_1,\ u_2+i u_3\right) \\ &=\left(\lvert z_1\rvert^2-\lvert z_2\rvert^2,\ 2 \bar{z}_1 z_2\right) . \end{aligned}\]

One checks that

\[\begin{aligned} \lvert\mathcal{K}\left(z_1, z_2\right)\rvert^2&=u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2 \\ &=\left(\lvert z_1\rvert^2+\lvert z_2\rvert^2\right)^2=I^2, \end{aligned}\]

where \(I = \lvert z_1\rvert^2 + \lvert z_2\rvert^2\) is the moment of inertia. So \(\mathcal{K} \circ \mathcal{J}\) sends the 3-sphere \(I = 1\) onto the unit 2-sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), and rotating the triangle (multiplying \((z_1, z_2)\) by \(e^{i\theta}\)) does not change the image. This is the Hopf fibration. The details are in Chenciner and Montgomery’s paper, A remarkable periodic solution of the three-body problem in the case of equal masses.

The figure-eight on the shape sphere

The sphere has a few landmarks. The collinear configurations form a great circle, the equator. The two poles are the equilateral triangles, one for each orientation. Three points on the equator, \(120^\circ\) apart, are the collisions of two bodies, and halfway between them are the three Euler configurations, in which one body sits at the midpoint of the other two.

The figure-eight orbit crosses the equator six times in each period, always at an Euler configuration, and stays well away from the collision points:

The Three-body gallery of Šuvakov and Dmitrašinović shows many other periodic orbits in the same representation.

Credits

This post is based on A. Chenciner and R. Montgomery, A remarkable periodic solution of the three-body problem in the case of equal masses, Annals of Mathematics 152 (2000), 881–901.

Revised on 25 October and 11 November 2026. The original called the quotient by rotations, which is homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the set of oriented similarity classes of triangles. Those are its congruence classes; the similarity classes form the shape sphere. The domain of the Jacobi map was written \(\mathcal{X}\) instead of \(X\), and Hopf was misspelt. The description of the landmarks on the sphere was added, and the paper is now linked on arXiv.
entry.summary: Reducing the planar three-body problem by translations, rotations and scaling: the Jacobi map, the Hopf map, and orbits drawn on the shape sphere.

entry.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I)

link.title: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I)

entry.content:
Part 4 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Ellipses and the Two-Body Problem
Next: Understanding and Visualising the Shape Sphere

This post introduces the problem of two fixed centres, also known as Euler’s three-body problem: a small body moving under the gravity of two masses held fixed in place. Unlike the general three-body problem, it is integrable.

Set-up

The two fixed masses \(m_\pm\) sit on the \(z\)-axis at \(z = \pm b\), and the third body moves in the \(x\)–\(z\) plane.

Simulation

To simulate the problem, I held two of the masses fixed and let the third move freely:

The Lagrangian

The natural coordinates are prolate spheroidal coordinates \((R, \sigma)\), which play the role of polar coordinates but with two foci:

\[x = \pm \sqrt{R^2-b^2}\, \sin \sigma, \qquad z = R \cos \sigma .\]

Writing \(\mathbf{r}(R, \sigma) = (x, z)\), the partial derivatives are

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial x}{\partial R} &= \pm \frac{R \sin \sigma}{\sqrt{R^2 - b^2}}, & \frac{\partial z}{\partial R} &= \cos \sigma, \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial \sigma} &= \pm \sqrt{R^2 - b^2}\, \cos \sigma, & \frac{\partial z}{\partial \sigma} &= -R \sin \sigma, \end{aligned}\]

so (taking the \(+\) sign)

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}_R &= \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial R} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{R \sin \sigma}{\sqrt{R^2 - b^2}} \\ \cos \sigma \end{pmatrix}, \\ \mathbf{r}_\sigma &= \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \sigma} = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{R^2 - b^2}\, \cos \sigma \\ -R \sin \sigma \end{pmatrix} . \end{aligned}\]

The metric components \(g_{RR}= \mathbf{r}_R \cdot \mathbf{r}_R\), \(g_{R\sigma} = \mathbf{r}_R\cdot\mathbf{r}_\sigma\) and \(g_{\sigma\sigma} = \mathbf{r}_\sigma\cdot\mathbf{r}_\sigma\) come out as

\[\begin{aligned} g_{RR}&=\frac{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma}{R^2-b^2}, \qquad g_{R \sigma}=0, \\ g_{\sigma \sigma}&=R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma . \end{aligned}\]

The distances to the two centres are \(R \mp b\cos\sigma\), so the potential energy per unit mass is

\[\begin{gathered} V=-\mu\, \frac{R+\beta b \cos \sigma}{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma}, \\ \mu = G(m_+ + m_-), \qquad \beta=\frac{m_{+}-m_{-}}{m_{+}+m_{-}} . \end{gathered}\]

The Lagrangian per unit mass is therefore

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L} = T-V &=\frac{1}{2}\, \frac{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma}{R^2-b^2}\, \dot{R}^2 \\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2}\left(R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma\right) \dot{\sigma}^2 \\ &\quad+\mu\, \frac{R+\beta b \cos \sigma}{R^2-b^2 \cos ^2 \sigma} . \end{aligned}\]

Jacobi elliptic functions

The equations of motion separate in these coordinates. Following the book, the equation for \(S = \cos\sigma\) reduces, after a change of independent variable from \(t\) to \(f\), to the form

\[S^{\prime 2}=\left(1-S^2\right)\left(1-k^2 S^2\right),\]

whose solution is

\[S=\operatorname{sn}(f+\omega \mid k).\]

Here \(\operatorname{sn}\) is one of the Jacobi elliptic functions. Trigonometric functions are defined with reference to a circle, and the Jacobi elliptic functions generalise them to other conic sections, in particular the ellipse.

To verify the solution, use

\[\frac{d}{du} \operatorname{sn}(u \mid k) = \operatorname{cn}(u \mid k) \operatorname{dn}(u \mid k)\]

together with the identities

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{sn}^2(u \mid k) + \operatorname{cn}^2(u \mid k) &= 1, \\ \operatorname{dn}^2(u \mid k) + k^2 \operatorname{sn}^2(u \mid k) &= 1 . \end{aligned}\]

With \(u = f + \omega\), these give \(\operatorname{cn}^2 u = 1 - S^2\) and \(\operatorname{dn}^2 u = 1 - k^2 S^2\), so

\[S'^2 = \operatorname{cn}^2(u \mid k)\, \operatorname{dn}^2(u \mid k) = (1 - S^2)(1 - k^2 S^2) .\]

Part 11 compares this solution with a simulated orbit.

Credits

This post is based on the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna. Parts of the material on Jacobi elliptic functions are from Wikipedia.

Revised on 25 October and 11 November 2026. Nothing in the results was wrong. The potential now comes with the definitions of \(\mu\) and \(\beta\), and the modulus is written \(k\) instead of \(k_{01}\). The note on the momentum bug moved to part 2, where the problem is described.
entry.summary: Euler's three-body problem: a test mass attracted by two fixed masses. Prolate spheroidal coordinates, the Lagrangian, and Jacobi elliptic functions.

entry.title: Ellipses and the Two-Body Problem
entry.content:
Part 3 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Symplectic Integrators
Next: Problem of Two Fixed Centres (Part I)

Before tackling three bodies, this post revisits ellipses and the Kepler problem.

Ellipses

Semi-major and semi-minor axes

I discussed the parametrisation of ellipses in an earlier post. An ellipse can be written as

\[\frac{X^2}{a^2}+\frac{Y^2}{b^2}=1,\]

with semi-major axis \(a\), semi-minor axis \(b\) and eccentricity \(e\), where

\[b^2=a^2(1-e^2).\]

Polar equations

Measured from the centre, at polar angle \(\theta_{\text{c}}\), the radius is

\[R= \frac{a \sqrt{1-e^2}}{\left(1-e^2 \cos^2\theta_{\text{c}}\right)^{1/2}} .\]

Measured from a focus, at polar angle \(\theta_{\text{f}}\), it is

\[r=\frac{a(1-e^2)}{1+e \cos\theta_{\text{f}}} = \frac{p}{1+e \cos\theta_{\text{f}}},\]

where \(p\) is the semi-latus rectum, which appeared in my post on Kepler’s third law.

The two-body problem

I have written about the reduction to relative motion and about two bodies falling straight towards each other. Here I focus on the shape of the orbits. Throughout, \(\mu = GM\) and \(\mathbf{r}\) is the relative position, which obeys \(\ddot{\mathbf{r}} = -\mu\,\mathbf{r}/r^3\).

Energy

The energy per unit (reduced) mass is conserved:

\[\frac{1}{2}v^2 - \frac{\mu}{r} = E .\]

Suppose \(E<0\) and write \(E=- \alpha^2\). Since \(\frac12 v^2 \ge 0\),

\[\begin{gathered} \frac{\mu}{r} \ge \alpha^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r \leq \frac{\mu}{\alpha^2} = 2a, \\ \text{where } a=\frac{\mu}{2 \alpha^2}. \end{gathered}\]

So negative energy implies a bounded orbit, and \(a\) turns out to be its semi-major axis.

Angular momentum and the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector

As shown in my post on Noether’s theorem, the angular momentum per unit mass, \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{r}\times\dot{\mathbf{r}}\), is conserved.

If \(\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{0}\), the motion is purely radial: the bodies move along a straight line, and collide if they are approaching. If \(\mathbf{C} \neq \mathbf{0}\), then \(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{C}=0\), so the motion lies in the fixed plane perpendicular to \(\mathbf{C}\).

Next, differentiate the unit vector \(\mathbf{e}_r = \mathbf{r}/r\):

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{d\mathbf{e}_r}{dt}&=\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{\mathbf{r}}{r}\right) =\frac{r \dot{\mathbf{r}}-\dot{r}\, \mathbf{r}}{r^2}=\frac{r^2 \dot{\mathbf{r}}-r \dot{r}\, \mathbf{r}}{r^3} \\ & =\frac{(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}) \dot{\mathbf{r}}-(\mathbf{r} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{r}}) \mathbf{r}}{r^3} \\ &=\frac{\mathbf{r} \times(\dot{\mathbf{r}} \times \mathbf{r})}{r^3}=\frac{\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{r}}{r^3}, \end{aligned}\]

using \(r\dot r = \mathbf{r}\cdot\dot{\mathbf{r}}\) and \(\dot{\mathbf{r}}\times\mathbf{r} = -\mathbf{C}\). Using the equation of motion, \(\mathbf{r}/r^3 = -\ddot{\mathbf{r}}/\mu\), and since \(\mathbf{C}\) is constant,

\[\frac{d\mathbf{e}_r}{dt}=-\frac{\mathbf{C} \times \ddot{\mathbf{r}}}{\mu}=-\frac{1}{\mu} \frac{d}{d t}(\mathbf{C} \times \dot{\mathbf{r}})=\frac{1}{\mu} \frac{d}{d t}(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{C}) .\]

Integrating, there is a constant vector \(\mathbf{e}\) such that

\[\mu\left(\mathbf{e}_r+\mathbf{e}\right)=\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{C} = \dot{\mathbf{r}} \times(\mathbf{r} \times \dot{\mathbf{r}})=v^2\, \mathbf{r}-r \dot{r}\, \dot{\mathbf{r}} .\]

Since \(\mathbf{C}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{e}_r\) and \(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{C}\), taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{C}\) gives \(\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{C}=0\): the vector \(\mathbf{e}\) lies in the plane of the motion.

The conserved vector \(\mathbf{e}\) is the eccentricity vector, a rescaling of the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector.

Kepler’s first law

Now take the dot product of the last equation with \(\mathbf{r}\). On the right, \((\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{C})\cdot\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{C}\cdot(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{v}) = C^2\). On the left, writing \(\theta\) for the angle between \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{e}\), we get \(\mu(r + e\, r\cos\theta)\). Hence

\[r = \frac{C^2/\mu}{1 + e\cos\theta},\]

which is exactly the polar equation of a conic with a focus at the origin, semi-latus rectum \(p = C^2/\mu\) and eccentricity \(e = \lvert\mathbf{e}\rvert\). Bound orbits (\(e<1\)) are ellipses: this is Kepler’s first law. The eccentricity vector points from the focus towards the point of closest approach.

The second and third laws are derived in my post on Kepler’s third law.

A hidden symmetry

By Noether’s theorem, a conserved quantity signals a symmetry, but for the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector the symmetry is hidden. For bound orbits, the Kepler problem is mathematically equivalent to free motion on a three-dimensional sphere in four-dimensional space, so its symmetry group is the group \(SO(4)\) of rotations in four dimensions, which is larger than the obvious rotations \(SO(3)\) of three-dimensional space.

Credits

This post is based on the book Integrable Systems in Celestial Mechanics by Diarmuid Ó’Mathúna. The remark about the four-dimensional sphere is based on Wikipedia.

Revised on 25 October 2026. Nothing in the results was wrong, but the bound \(r \le 2a\) was stated without its derivation, and the derivation of the eccentricity vector stopped before reaching the orbit equation. Both are now complete, with \(\mu = GM\) throughout.
entry.summary: Polar equations of the ellipse, bound orbits from negative energy, and the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector, which gives Kepler's first law.

entry.title: Symplectic Integrators
entry.content:
Part 2 of 11 of the research log of my 2024 summer project on the three-body problem, at the University of Edinburgh, supervised by Prof. Jenni Smillie.

Previous: Plotting and Visualising the Three-Body Problem
Next: Ellipses and the Two-Body Problem

This post explains what makes an integrator symplectic, and compares second-, third- and fourth-order symplectic schemes on the figure-eight orbit.

What is a symplectic integrator?

Start from Liouville’s theorem in Hamiltonian mechanics: the flow of a Hamiltonian system preserves phase-space volume. For one degree of freedom, a small region of the \((x, p)\) plane keeps the same area as it evolves, \(dA = dA'\):

So evolving Newton’s equations forward by a finite time defines an area-preserving (more generally, symplectic) map of phase space. A symplectic integrator is a numerical method whose single step is itself a symplectic map.

This matters for long simulations. A symplectic integrator does not conserve the energy exactly. What it conserves, up to an error that shrinks exponentially as the step is reduced, is a slightly modified (“shadow”) Hamiltonian, so the computed energy oscillates within a fixed band instead of drifting. Non-symplectic methods such as the explicit Euler method and RK4 show a steady energy drift.

Checking whether a scheme is symplectic

For one degree of freedom, write a step of a linear scheme as

\[\begin{pmatrix} x_{n+1} \\ p_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}=A\begin{pmatrix} x_n \\ p_n \end{pmatrix}.\]

The scheme is symplectic if and only if \(\det A = 1\). For a nonlinear scheme the same test is applied to the Jacobian of the map, and in higher dimensions the condition becomes \(M^{T}JM = J\) for the Jacobian \(M\) and the standard symplectic matrix \(J\).

Higher-order schemes

A family of explicit symplectic schemes splits each time step \(\Delta t\) into \(n\) stages. Stage \(i\) first moves the positions with the current velocities (a drift) and then updates the velocities with the accelerations at the new positions (a kick):

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{i}&=\mathbf{x}_{i-1}+c_i\, \mathbf{v}_{i-1}\, \Delta t, \\ \mathbf{v}_{i}&=\mathbf{v}_{i-1}+d_i\, \mathbf{a}\left(\mathbf{x}_{i}\right) \Delta t . \end{aligned}\]

Each drift and each kick is a symplectic map, so their composition is symplectic as well, and the coefficients \(c_i\) and \(d_i\) set the order of accuracy. Velocity Verlet is the case \(c = (0, 1)\), \(d = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\). A third-order scheme (Ruth) uses

\[c = \left(1, -\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}\right), \qquad d = \left(-\tfrac{1}{24}, \tfrac{3}{4}, \tfrac{7}{24}\right),\]

and a fourth-order scheme (Forest–Ruth) uses

\[\begin{aligned} c &= \biggl(\frac{1}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})},\ \frac{1 - 2^{1/3}}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})}, \\ &\qquad \frac{1 - 2^{1/3}}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})},\ \frac{1}{2(2 - 2^{1/3})}\biggr), \\ d &= \left(\frac{1}{2 - 2^{1/3}},\ -\frac{2^{1/3}}{2 - 2^{1/3}},\ \frac{1}{2 - 2^{1/3}},\ 0\right). \end{aligned}\]

The order of the two updates within a stage matters. With these coefficients, kicking before drifting is still symplectic but much less accurate than Verlet: on the test below its energy deviation is of order \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-2}\).

Accuracy of the higher-order schemes

I integrated the figure-eight orbit for \(50\,000\) steps with \(\Delta t = 0.01\), about 79 periods, and recorded the energy deviation \((E_{\max} - E_{\min})/\lvert E_0\rvert\):

Scheme Order Energy deviation
Velocity Verlet 2 \(5.9 \times 10^{-5}\)
Ruth 3 \(4.1 \times 10^{-8}\)
Forest–Ruth 4 \(1.9 \times 10^{-8}\)

The higher-order schemes improve the energy conservation by more than three orders of magnitude, at three force evaluations per step where Verlet needs one. Spending the same effort on Verlet, with a step three times smaller, reduces its deviation only by a factor of nine, to \(6.6 \times 10^{-6}\).

Momentum conservation

Every kick adds equal and opposite impulses to each pair of bodies, so all of these schemes should conserve the total linear momentum to round-off precision. In the first version of my code they did not. The error was small, but it grew steadily with time:

The cause was a bug in the code, not the integrator: the variable that accumulates the momentum components was not reset to zero at each time step. After the fix the error stays at the level of floating-point round-off:

A perturbed figure-eight

Starting close to the figure-eight, but not on it, gives an orbit that keeps the figure-eight shape for many periods while the whole pattern slowly rotates:

Credits

The section on the definition of symplectic integrators, including the figure, is based on these notes on the leapfrog method by Peter Young.

Revised on 25 October and 11 November 2026. The numbers were right, but the original wrote each stage as a kick followed by a drift. With the coefficients quoted, that order gives a much less accurate scheme. The code moved the positions first, which is the order now given, and it reproduces the energy deviations in the table. The definition of the energy deviation and the cause of the momentum error (moved here from part 4) were added, and the errors are rounded to two figures.
entry.summary: Why area-preserving (symplectic) integrators keep the energy error bounded, and how third- and fourth-order schemes improve on Verlet for the figure-eight orbit.
